---
title: "Read your data"
description: "Turn a tracking export into an aniframe with aniread — and grab bundled sample data to follow along."
order: 3
---

[aniread](https://animovement.dev/aniread) reads movement data from a wide range
of sources — video-based pose estimation, centroid trackers, motion capture,
even hardware trackballs — and hands you back a tidy
[aniframe](movement-data.qmd). Every source has a dedicated `read_*()` function,
and they all return the same structure, so the rest of your pipeline doesn't
care where the data came from.

## Grab some sample data {#sec-sample}

You don't need your own files to follow along. `get_sample_data()` downloads a
real example export for any supported source and returns the path to the
downloaded file:

```r
library(animovement)

path <- get_sample_data("deeplabcut")
path
#> "/tmp/RtmpXXXX/deeplabcut_sample.csv"
```

To see everything that's available, call it with `list_datasets = TRUE`:

```r
get_sample_data(list_datasets = TRUE)
```

Some sources ship more than one dataset; pick one with the `dataset` argument
(and pass a permanent `cache_dir` if you'd like the download to persist across
sessions):

```r
path <- get_sample_data("sleap", dataset = "single_fly")
```

You can even point it at any URL to pull a file from a remote source:

```r
path <- get_sample_data("https://example.com/my_tracking_file.csv")
```

See the full reference for
[`get_sample_data()`](https://animovement.dev/aniread/reference/get_sample_data.html).

## Read it into an aniframe {#sec-read}

Feed that path to the matching reader. For our DeepLabCut sample:

```r
movement <- read_deeplabcut(path)

movement
#> # Individuals: 1
#> # Keypoints:   snout, leftear, rightear, tailbase
#> ...
```

The result is a standard aniframe — ready for
[checking and processing](process-data.qmd).

::: {.callout-note}
## Image coordinates are flipped for you
Pose-estimation tools such as DeepLabCut store positions in *image* coordinates,
where `y` grows *downward* from the top-left. `read_deeplabcut()` reflects `y`
so the aniframe uses the conventional bottom-left origin. If your export doesn't
record the video resolution, pass `video_height =` (in pixels) for an accurate
flip; otherwise the reader falls back to the largest `y` value it sees.
:::

## Pick the right reader {#sec-readers}

The reader name matches the source. A few of the most common:

| Source | Function |
|--------|----------|
| DeepLabCut | `read_deeplabcut()` |
| SLEAP | `read_sleap()` |
| idtracker.ai | `read_idtracker()` |
| LightningPose | `read_lightningpose()` |
| Anipose (3-D) | `read_anipose()` |
| Trackball hardware | `read_trackball()` |
| BORIS annotations | `read_boris()` |

Swap the reader, keep the rest of your workflow identical — that's the whole
point of a shared data structure:

```r
# Same pipeline, different source
movement <- read_sleap(get_sample_data("sleap"))
```

For the complete list of sources and their file formats, call:

```r
get_supported_sources()
#> # A tibble: 18 × 3
#>   source       reader              suffix
#>   <chr>        <chr>               <chr>
#> 1 deeplabcut   read_deeplabcut     csv, h5
#> 2 sleap        read_sleap          h5
#> # … with 16 more rows
```

## Reading your own files {#sec-own}

Once you're ready, replace `get_sample_data()` with a path to your own export:

```r
movement <- read_deeplabcut("~/experiments/session01/DLC_output.csv")
```

Have a format aniread doesn't cover yet? `read_custom()` lets you map arbitrary
columns onto the aniframe slots, and `write_aniframe()` saves any aniframe to a
fast Parquet file you can re-open with `read_aniframe()`.
